claim: Adiponectin is an adipocyte-derived hormone exerting pleiotropic beneficial effects on metabolism.
source: Adiponectin is an adipocyte-derived hormone exerting pleiotropic beneficial effects on metabolism (Ye and Scherer, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ye and Scherer, 2013

claim: Increased circulating adiponectin improves the metabolic flexibility of adipose tissue and confers systemic tolerance to obesity.
source: Increased circulating adiponectin improves the metabolic flexibility of adipose tissue and confers systemic tolerance to obesity (Asterholm and Scherer, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Asterholm and Scherer, 2010

claim: Under normal physiological conditions, adiponectin promotes plasma lipid clearance.
source: Under normal physiological conditions, adiponectin promotes plasma lipid clearance (Combs et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Combs et al., 2004 and Qiao et al., 2008

claim: Adiponectin is not essential for life under normal physiological conditions.
source: Paradoxically however, even though many important functions have been attributed to this circulating factor in mice and humans (Shetty et al., 2009; Turer and Scherer, 2012), adiponectin is not essential for life under normal physiological conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Shetty et al., 2009 and Turer and Scherer, 2012

claim: Genetic deletion of adiponectin in rodents leads to mild or moderate insulin resistance, which is exacerbated upon high-fat diet challenge.
source: Genetic deletion of adiponectin in rodents leads to mild or moderate insulin resistance, which is exacerbated upon high-fat diet challenge (Kubota et al., 2002; Maeda et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kubota et al., 2002 and Maeda et al., 2002

claim: Adiponectin is required for PPARγ agonist-mediated improvements in insulin sensitivity.
source: Adiponectin is required for PPARγ agonist-mediated improvements in insulin sensitivity (Nawrocki et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nawrocki et al., 2006

claim: The failure of insulin-producing β-cells is a hallmark of the pathophysiology of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
source: The failure of insulin-producing β-cells is a hallmark of the pathophysiology of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about diabetes pathophysiology

claim: The ongoing loss of β-cells under diabetic conditions is associated with a failure to effectively regenerate β-cell mass.
source: The ongoing loss of β-cells under these conditions is associated with a failure to effectively regenerate β-cell mass.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about β-cell regeneration in diabetes

claim: The low capacity for β-cell replication and differentiation contributes to the failure to regenerate β-cell mass.
source: This can be attributed not only to the low capacity for replication and differentiation (Bouwens and Rooman, 2005) but also the detrimental cytotoxic environment that the cells are exposed to due to the dysregulation of the balance between insulin and glucagon (Robertson, 2009; Unger and Cherrington, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bouwens and Rooman, 2005; Robertson, 2009; Unger and Cherrington, 2012

claim: Insulin deficiency results in hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia, both of which trigger β-cell glucotoxicity and oxidative stress.
source: Insulin deficiency results in hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia, both of which trigger β-cell glucotoxicity and oxidative stress (Poitout and Robertson, 2008), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Fonseca et al., 2009), and lipotoxicity (Kusminski et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Poitout and Robertson, 2008; Fonseca et al., 2009; Kusminski et al., 2009

claim: Tissue culture data suggested that adiponectin regulates β-cell viability.
source: Tissue culture data suggested that adiponectin regulates β-cell viability (Brown et al., 2010; Holland et al., 2011; Rao et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 2010; Holland et al., 2011; Rao et al., 2012

claim: Adiponectin protects β-cells against lipotoxicity and apoptosis, both in cultured cells and in vivo.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that adiponectin protects β-cells against lipotoxicity and apoptosis, both in cultured cells and in vivo (Holland et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holland et al., 2011

claim: After extensive β-cell ablation in the PANIC-ATTAC model, adiponectin becomes essential for survival.
source: In this study, we took advantage of the PANIC-ATTAC transgenic mouse model (Wang et al., 2008). After extensive β-cell ablation, adiponectin becomes essential for survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citation to Wang et al., 2008

claim: In the context of insulin deficiency, the lack of adiponectin aggravates the lipoatrophy and hyperlipidemia to lethal levels.
source: In the context of insulin deficiency, the lack of adiponetin aggravates the lipoatrophy and hyperlipidemia to lethal levels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased mortality in adiponectin null mice after β-cell ablation

claim: Adiponectin is required for lipid uptake into subcutaneous white adipose tissue under insulinopenic conditions.
source: Specifically, adiponectin is required for lipid uptake into subcutaneous white adipose tissue.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 3H-triolein uptake assays and BODIPY-labeled fatty acid experiments

claim: Under insulinopenic conditions, the primary adiponectin-mediated effect relies on enhanced insulin sensitivity and endocytic activity.
source: However, under insulinopenic conditions, the primary adiponectin-mediated effect relies on enhanced insulin sensitivity and endocytic activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing insulin signaling changes and vesicle density measurements

claim: Adiponectin overexpressing mice effectively overcome intracellular lipotoxicity in β-cells by ameliorating lipid metabolism.
source: While insulin deficiency and widespread loss of β-cells lead to augmented intracellular lipotoxicity, adiponectin overexpressing mice effectively overcome the resulting intracellular lipotoxicity in β-cells by ameliorating lipid metabolism and thereby paving the way for β-cell mass recovery.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced ceramide levels in islets from adiponectin transgenic mice

claim: Augmentation of adiponectin is sufficient to promote β-cell regeneration.
source: Our findings reveal a novel role of adiponectin as a housekeeping protein under insulinopenic conditions, and augmentation of adiponectin is sufficient to promote β-cell regeneration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing β-cell mass recovery in adiponectin transgenic mice

claim: P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice started with similar β-cell mass before dimerizer treatment.
source: Starting with similar β-cell mass (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), 8-week old male homozygous PANIC-ATTACs with adiponectin wild type (P-Adn+/+) or knockout (P-Adn−/−) were treated with the same high-dose of dimerizer AP20187 to induce caspase-8-mediated apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: 2 weeks after the initial dimerizer administration, the insulin positive areas of P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice decreased down to <15% of their starting levels.
source: 2 weeks after the initial dimerizer administration, the insulin positive areas of P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice decreased down to <15% of their starting levels and further decreased down to <10% around 10 weeks post β-cell ablation (Figure 1A and Figure1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Both the P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice showed sustained glucose levels above ∼500 mg/dl after β-cell ablation.
source: In this setting, both the P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice showed sustained glucose levels above ∼500 mg/dl (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Fasting insulin levels decreased to <8% of the euglycemic wild-type controls after parallel dimerizer treatment in both P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice.
source: Their fasting insulin levels decreased to <8% of the euglycemic wild-type (WT) controls after parallel dimerizer treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Both the P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice were severely glucose intolerant after intensive β-cell ablation.
source: With such intensive β-cell ablation and insulin deficiency, both the P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice were severely glucose intolerant (Figure 1D), and their glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) was abolished (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D and 1E

claim: P-Adn−/− mice showed a dramatically lower survival rate than P-Adn+/+ mice under insulinopenic conditions.
source: To our surprise, under the insulinopenic conditions, P-Adn−/− mice showed a dramatically lower survival rate than P-Adn+/+ mice (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Only 33% of the adiponectin null mice survived 9 weeks post dimerizer, with a median survival of 8.4 weeks.
source: Only 33% of the adiponectin null mice survived 9 weeks post dimerizer, with a median survival of 8.4 weeks, while 87% of the P-Adn+/+ mice remained alive.
evidence: Supported by survival data from the experiment

claim: 87% of the P-Adn+/+ mice remained alive 9 weeks post dimerizer.
source: Only 33% of the adiponectin null mice survived 9 weeks post dimerizer, with a median survival of 8.4 weeks, while 87% of the P-Adn+/+ mice remained alive.
evidence: Supported by survival data from the experiment

claim: Adiponectin overexpressing mice (P-AdnTg/+) show a similar survival rate as P-Adn+/+ mice after β-cell ablation.
source: Adiponectin overexpressing mice (Combs et al., 2004) crossed into the homozygous PANIC-ATTAC background (P-AdnTg/+) show a similar survival rate as P-Adn+/+ mice.
evidence: Supported by survival data and citation to Combs et al., 2004

claim: The fivefold increased mortality in P-Adn−/− mice was associated with an extreme deterioration in lipid metabolism.
source: This fivefold increased mortality in P-Adn−/− mice was associated with an extreme deterioration in lipid metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the survival data and lipid metabolism measurements

claim: Triglyceride levels in P-Adn−/− mice (6.8 ± 1.0 mM) were 60% higher than the levels in P-Adn+/+ mice.
source: Their triglyceride levels (6.8 ± 1.0 mM) were 60% higher than the levels in P-Adn+/+ mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Circulating ketone bodies in the adiponectin null mice reached an aberrantly high level (0.77 ± 0.15 mM), which was sixfold higher than the WT level and 3.5-fold higher than the P-Adn+/+ level.
source: More strikingly, the circulating ketone bodies in the adiponectin null mice reached an aberrantly high level (0.77 ± 0.15 mM), which was sixfold higher than the WT level and 3.5-fold higher than the P-Adn+/+ level (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1H

claim: P-Adn−/− mice demonstrated a significant decrease in fat mass, to a critically low level of <5% body weight.
source: Prior to the aggravated hyperlipidemia, P-Adn−/− mice demonstrated a significant decrease in fat mass, to a critically low level of <5% body weight (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: No significant difference in food intake was observed between P-Adn−/− and P-Adn+/+ mice.
source: We observed no significant difference in food intake between P-Adn−/− and P-Adn+/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: STZ-treated adiponectin null mice had significantly lower adipose tissue mass than WT mice.
source: Consistent with the observations in the PANIC-ATTAC model (Figure 1I), STZ-treated adiponectin null mice had significantly lower adipose tissue mass than WT mice (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Circulating triglyceride levels in STZ-treated Adn−/− mice showed a 2.3-fold increase in fed mice compared to Adn+/+ mice.
source: The deterioration in lipid metabolism in the STZ-treated Adn−/− mice was also apparent as judged by the increase in circulating triglyceride levels in fed mice (2.3-fold) (Figure 2B), overnight fasted mice (3.6-fold) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), and following an oral triglyceride load (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Circulating triglyceride levels in STZ-treated Adn−/− mice showed a 3.6-fold increase in overnight fasted mice compared to Adn+/+ mice.
source: The deterioration in lipid metabolism in the STZ-treated Adn−/− mice was also apparent as judged by the increase in circulating triglyceride levels in fed mice (2.3-fold) (Figure 2B), overnight fasted mice (3.6-fold) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), and following an oral triglyceride load (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: Non-esterified fatty acids (NEFAs) levels were higher in STZ-treated Adn−/− mice (1.4-fold increase).
source: Non-esterified fatty acids (NEFAs) levels were also higher in Adn−/− mice (1.4-fold increase) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: The plasma lipoprotein fractionation of STZ-treated Adn−/− mice displayed elevated triglyceride and cholesterol content in VLDL.
source: The plasma lipoprotein fractionation of STZ-treated Adn−/− mice displayed elevated triglyceride and cholesterol content in VLDL (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E

claim: Exogenous administration of adiponectin induced a lowering of circulating triglycerides in STZ-treated Adn−/− mice.
source: In an attempt to rescue this phenotype not only genetically, but also using a recombinant protein approach, exogenous administration of adiponectin induced a lowering of circulating triglycerides in STZ-treated Adn−/− mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Adiponectin null mice demonstrated only a minor trend towards an increase in serum triglyceride content after tyloxapol injection compared to WT control mice.
source: Compared to WT control mice, adiponectin null mice demonstrated only a minor trend towards an increase in serum triglyceride content (Figure 2F) and rate of accumulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: No significant changes were observed in a panel of metabolic gene expression in the livers of STZ-treated Adn+/+ and Adn−/− mice.
source: We also examined a panel of metabolic gene expression in the livers of STZ-treated Adn+/+ and Adn−/− mice and observed no significant changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: A low dose of insulin (0.1 mU/g body weight) substantially reduced serum glycerol in STZ-treated mice.
source: This small amount of insulin substantially reduced serum glycerol (Figure 2G), while it only minimally affected circulating triglycerides (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A) and NEFAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Adiponectin null mice were resistant to the action of insulin on glycerol levels, with minimal impact on glycerol levels.
source: Intriguingly, compared to WT mice, adiponectin null mice were resistant to the action of insulin, with minimal impact on glycerol levels (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Adiponectin is critical for insulin-mediated suppression of lipolysis under insulinopenic conditions.
source: This suggests adiponectin is critical for insulin-mediated suppression of lipolysis under insulinopenic conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the insulin resistance to glycerol suppression in adiponectin null mice

claim: The enhanced lipolysis in STZ-treated adiponectin null mice might, at least in part, account for the reduced fat mass seen in the Adn−/− mice.
source: The enhanced lipolysis in STZ-treated adiponectin null mice might, at least in part, account for the reduced fat mass seen in the Adn−/− mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the lipolysis and fat mass data

claim: No apparent differences in whole body triolein clearance between WT and adiponectin null mice were noted prior to STZ treatment.
source: No apparent differences between WT and adiponectin null mice were noted prior to STZ treatment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 3H-triolein uptake assays

claim: Post STZ treatment, adiponectin null mice showed a 39% lower whole body clearance rate of labeled triolein compared to WT mice.
source: In contrast, post STZ treatment, adiponectin null mice showed a 39% lower whole body clearance rate of labeled triolein compared to WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Significant differences of triolein uptake were observed only in the subcutaneous white adipose tissue (50% lower in STZ-treated null mice than in STZ-treated WT mice) among the nine tissues examined.
source: Among the nine tissues examined, we observed significant differences of triolein uptake only in the subcutaneous white adipose tissue (WAT, 50% lower in STZ-treated null mice than in STZ-treated WT mice) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: After long-term high-fat diet exposure, adiponectin promotes preferentially subcutaneous WAT expansion.
source: Consistent with a primary site of action on subcutaneous fat pads, we have reported that after long-term high-fat diet exposure, adiponectin promotes preferentially subcutaneous WAT expansion (Asterholm and Scherer, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Asterholm and Scherer, 2010

claim: The difference in triolein uptake in subcutaneous WAT was primarily the result of a reduced level of incorporation.
source: The difference in triolein uptake in subcutaneous WAT was primarily the result of a reduced level of incorporation.
evidence: Supported by data partitioning tissue-specific 3H-triolein uptake into incorporated vs oxidized lipids

claim: Histological analysis of adiponectin knockouts demonstrated a major reduction of adipocyte size in subcutaneous WAT and trends towards smaller cell size in brown adipose tissue.
source: In agreement with the 3H-triolein uptake assay, histological analysis of adiponectin knockouts demonstrated a major reduction of adipocyte size in subcutaneous WAT and trends towards smaller cell size in brown adipose tissue (BAT).
evidence: Supported by histological data

claim: No reduction in adipocyte size was found in gonadal WAT of adiponectin knockouts.
source: However, no such reduction was found in gonadal WAT (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Adiponectin overexpression dramatically enhanced BODIPY signal in adipocytes, while adiponectin nulls showed a significant reduction.
source: Adiponectin overexpression dramatically enhanced BODIPY signal in adipocytes, while adiponectin nulls showed a significant reduction (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: STZ-treated animals showed elevated signals for apolipoproteins compared to the euglycemic wild-type controls.
source: Compared to the euglycemic wild-type controls, STZ-treated animals showed elevated signals for apolipoproteins.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data for apolipoproteins

claim: Most of the ApoA1 and ApoE signals, as well as part of the ApoB signal, located adjacent to endomucin, a marker for venous and capillary endothelial cells, reflecting apolipoproteins in circulation.
source: Interestingly, most of the ApoA1 and ApoE signals, as well as part of the ApoB signal, located adjacent to endomucin, a marker for venous and capillary endothelial cells, reflecting apolipoproteins in circulation.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence co-staining data

claim: The endomucin signal demonstrated increased vascular density in subcutaneous WAT of STZ-treated lipoatrophic animals.
source: The endomucin signal itself demonstrated increased vascular density in subcutaneous WAT of STZ-treated lipoatrophic animals, which was also observed in gonadal WAT (Figure 3—figure supplement 3–5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3–5

claim: Adiponectin knockout-induced ApoA1 accumulation was significant in subcutaneous WAT and BAT, but not in gonadal WAT.
source: Furthermore, adiponectin knockout-induced ApoA1 accumulation was significant in subcutaneous WAT and BAT, but not in gonadal WAT (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Compared to STZ-treated wild-type mice, adiponectin null mice showed trends towards an increase in ApoB signal in both subcutaneous and gonadal WATs.
source: Compared to STZ-treated wild-type mice, adiponectin null mice showed trends towards an increase in ApoB signal in both subcutaneous and gonadal WATs (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: There was a trend towards an increase in ApoE signal in subcutaneous WAT, but not in gonadal WAT.
source: As for the ApoE signal, there was a trend towards an increase in subcutaneous WAT, but not in gonadal WAT (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 5

claim: There is an overall accumulation of apolipoproteins in the local circulation of adipose tissues of STZ-treated mice, which is exacerbated by adiponectin depletion predominantly in subcutaneous WAT.
source: Collectively, these data suggest an overall accumulation of apolipoproteins in the local circulation of adipose tissues of STZ-treated mice, which is exacerbated by adiponectin depletion predominantly in subcutaneous WAT.
evidence: Inferred from the apolipoprotein immunofluorescence data

claim: A low dose of insulin treatment (0.2 mU/g body weight) markedly suppressed the hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) serine-660 phosphorylation by 57% in subcutaneous WAT of STZ-treated wild-type mice.
source: A low dose of insulin treatment (0.2 mU/g body weight) markedly suppressed the hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) serine-660 phosphorylation, a marker positively associated with lipolysis, by 57% and induced Akt serine-473 phosphorylation by 8.6-fold in subcutaneous WAT of STZ-treated wild-type mice.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: A low dose of insulin treatment (0.2 mU/g body weight) induced Akt serine-473 phosphorylation by 8.6-fold in subcutaneous WAT of STZ-treated wild-type mice.
source: A low dose of insulin treatment (0.2 mU/g body weight) markedly suppressed the hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) serine-660 phosphorylation, a marker positively associated with lipolysis, by 57% and induced Akt serine-473 phosphorylation by 8.6-fold in subcutaneous WAT of STZ-treated wild-type mice.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: STZ-treated adiponectin nulls showed a blunted response in HSL inhibition (41%) compared to wild-type mice.
source: However, STZ-treated adiponectin nulls showed a blunted response in HSL inhibition (41%), and an abolished Akt activation (13%), as compared to the same animal prior to insulin injection (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: STZ-treated adiponectin nulls showed an abolished Akt activation (13%) compared to wild-type mice.
source: However, STZ-treated adiponectin nulls showed a blunted response in HSL inhibition (41%), and an abolished Akt activation (13%), as compared to the same animal prior to insulin injection (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The unchanged post-heparin lipoprotein lipase activity is unlikely to be a major contributing factor to the impaired lipid uptake in the STZ-treated adiponectin null animals.
source: The unchanged post-heparin lipoprotein lipase activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) is unlikely to be a major contributing factor to the impaired lipid uptake in the STZ-treated adiponectin null animals.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The fatty acid translocase CD36 shows comparable distributions between genotypes.
source: The fatty acid translocase CD36 (Figure 4B) and fatty acid transport protein 1 (FATP1) (Figure 4C) are also unlikely contributors, both of which show comparable distributions between genotypes.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Fatty acid transport protein 1 (FATP1) shows comparable distributions between genotypes.
source: The fatty acid translocase CD36 (Figure 4B) and fatty acid transport protein 1 (FATP1) (Figure 4C) are also unlikely contributors, both of which show comparable distributions between genotypes.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Expression of Scavenger Receptor Class B Member 1 (SR-B1), a high-density lipoprotein (HDL) receptor, was enhanced in STZ-treated adiponectin knockouts.
source: Expression of Scavenger Receptor Class B Member 1 (SR-B1), a high-density lipoprotein (HDL) receptor, was enhanced in STZ-treated adiponectin knockouts (Figure 4D), which could reflect a compensatory response for the HDL accumulation in circulation (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The enhanced SR-B1 expression could reflect a compensatory response for the HDL accumulation in circulation.
source: Expression of Scavenger Receptor Class B Member 1 (SR-B1), a high-density lipoprotein (HDL) receptor, was enhanced in STZ-treated adiponectin knockouts (Figure 4D), which could reflect a compensatory response for the HDL accumulation in circulation (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on SR-B1 expression and HDL accumulation data

claim: A twofold increase in the linear density of vesicular structures associated with the plasma membrane of the subcutaneous adipocytes was observed in the wild-type mice after STZ treatment.
source: Employing transmission electron microscopy, we observed a twofold increase in the linear density of vesicular structures associated with the plasma membrane of the subcutaneous adipocytes in the wild-type mice after STZ treatment.
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and 4F

claim: The upregulation of vesicle density was abolished in the adiponectin nulls.
source: In contrast, this upregulation of vesicle density was abolished in the adiponectin nulls (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and 4F

claim: STZ treatment enhanced mitochondrial density in both Adn+/+ and Adn−/− mice.
source: Interestingly, STZ treatment enhanced mitochondrial density in both Adn+/+ and Adn−/− mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), consistent with the 3H-triolein oxidation capacity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Caveolin-1 was detectable in the majority of subcutaneous adipocytes in wildtype mice after STZ treatment.
source: Caveolin-1, one of the major components in the plasma membrane and trans-Golgi network, was detectable in the majority of subcutaneous adipocytes in wildtype mice after STZ treatment.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G

claim: In STZ-treated adiponectin null mice, the caveolin-1 signal was almost completely depleted in subcutaneous adipocytes, and the majority of the signal was associated with the endomucin-positive endothelial cells.
source: In contrast, in STZ-treated adiponectin null mice, the caveolin-1 signal was almost completely depleted in subcutaneous adipocytes, and the majority of the signal was associated with the endomucin-positive endothelial cells (Figure 4G) under those conditions.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G

claim: The caveolin-1 changes were not observed in either the euglycemic controls or the gonadal WAT.
source: These changes were not observed in either the euglycemic controls or the gonadal WAT (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G and 4H

claim: Under conditions of limited insulin availability, adiponectin plays an important role in potentiating insulin sensitivity, supporting endocytic activity for triglyceride, and promoting lipid storage specifically in subcutaneous WAT.
source: These findings suggest that under conditions of limited insulin availability, adiponectin plays an important role in potentiating insulin sensitivity, supporting endocytic activity for triglyceride, and promoting lipid storage specifically in subcutaneous WAT.
evidence: Inferred from the insulin signaling, vesicle density, and lipid uptake data

claim: The lack of adiponectin exacerbates lipoatrophy and hyperlipidemia, and this may be due–at least in part–to the diminished insulin signaling and the selective loss of the caveolin-1 complex.
source: The lack of adiponectin exacerbates lipoatrophy and hyperlipidemia, and this may be due–at least in part–to the diminished insulin signaling and the selective loss of the caveolin-1 complex.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the insulin signaling and caveolin-1 data

claim: The adiponectin transgenic mice sustained higher levels of plasma adiponectin than the wild-type mice, also in the absence of insulin.
source: The adiponectin transgenic mice sustained higher levels of plasma adiponectin than the wild-type mice, also in the absence of insulin (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Dimerizer treatment led to a moderate decrease in whole-body fat mass by week 2 in adiponectin transgenic mice.
source: Dimerizer treatment led to a moderate decrease in whole-body fat mass by week 2.
evidence: Supported by body composition data

claim: From week 2 onward, the adiponectin transgenic mice showed a complete recovery in fat mass by week 5 and sustained normal fat mass through week 10.
source: From that point onward, the adiponectin transgenic mice showed a complete recovery in fat mass by week 5 and sustained normal fat mass through week 10, at which point the experiment was stopped (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Early post β-cell ablation, P-AdnTg/+ mice already showed significant improvements during a triglyceride tolerance test compared to P-Adn+/+ mice.
source: Early post β-cell ablation, P-AdnTg/+ mice already showed significant improvements during a triglyceride tolerance test compared to P-Adn+/+ mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The baseline serum triglyceride levels were significantly lower in P-AdnTg/+ mice compared to P-Adn+/+ mice at all stages.
source: Furthermore, the baseline serum triglyceride levels were significantly lower in P-AdnTg/+ mice compared to P-Adn+/+ mice at all stages (Figure 5D), indicative of the powerful lipid-lowering effects of adiponectin on the clearance of circulating triglycerides.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D

claim: P-AdnTg/+ mice restored their serum ketone bodies to a level (0.12 ± 0.02 mM) comparable to unchallenged WT controls (0.13 ± 0.01 mM) and significantly lower than both the P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice.
source: Subsequently, P-AdnTg/+ mice restored their serum ketone bodies to a level (0.12 ± 0.02 mM) comparable to unchallenged WT controls (0.13 ± 0.01 mM) and significantly lower than both the P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Trends towards a decrease in NEFAs were observed in adiponectin transgenic mice.
source: We also observed trends towards a decrease in NEFAs in adiponectin transgenic mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Increasing circulating adiponectin is sufficient to improve systemic lipid metabolism and promote fat mass recovery in the context of insulinopenic diabetes.
source: Our findings suggest that increasing circulating adiponectin is sufficient to improve systemic lipid metabolism and promote fat mass recovery in the context of insulinopenic diabetes.
evidence: Inferred from the lipid metabolism and fat mass data in adiponectin transgenic mice

claim: For most individual ceramide species as well as the total ceramide content, there was a trend in diabetic P-Adn+/+ islets towards increased ceramides as compared to islets from euglycemic WT mice and a concomitant drop of ceramides in the P-AdnTg/+ islets.
source: For most individual ceramide species as well as the total ceramide content, we observed a trend in diabetic P-Adn+/+ islets towards increased ceramides as compared to islets from euglycemic WT mice and a concomitant drop of ceramides in the P-AdnTg/+ islets (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by sphingolipid mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The same trends as ceramides applied to dihydro-ceramides, which are ceramide biosynthetic precursors.
source: The same trends applied to dihydro-ceramides, which are ceramide biosynthetic precursors (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by sphingolipid mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Among the hexosyl-ceramides, lactosyl-ceramides displayed the same pattern of change as ceramides overall.
source: Among the hexosyl-ceramides, lactosyl-ceramides displayed the same pattern of change as ceramides overall (Figure 6C), while no significant changes were observed in glucosyl-ceramides (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by sphingolipid mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6C

claim: No significant changes were observed in glucosyl-ceramides among the three genotypes.
source: Among the hexosyl-ceramides, lactosyl-ceramides displayed the same pattern of change as ceramides overall (Figure 6C), while no significant changes were observed in glucosyl-ceramides (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by sphingolipid mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Most of the sphingomyelins reproduced the trends seen in ceramides among the three genotypes.
source: As the major storage pool of sphingolipids, most of the sphingomyelins also reproduced the trends seen in ceramides among the three genotypes (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by sphingolipid mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6E

claim: The increased levels of lipotoxic species in P-Adn+/+ islets may account, at least in part, for the further loss of β-cells from week 5 to week 10 post the initial insult.
source: Taken together, our data suggest increased levels of lipotoxic species in P-Adn+/+ islets, which may account, at least in part, for the further loss of β-cells from week 5 to week 10 post the initial insult (Figure 1A).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on sphingolipid data and β-cell mass data

claim: Adiponectin transgenic mice reduced the lipotoxic sphingolipid content to levels seen in the non-diabetic WT mice.
source: In contrast, adiponectin transgenic mice reduced the lipotoxic sphingolipid content to levels seen in the non-diabetic WT mice.
evidence: Supported by sphingolipid mass spectrometry data

claim: The reduced level of local lipotoxicity may mediate β-cell survival and proliferation.
source: The reduced level of local lipotoxicity may mediate β-cell survival and proliferation.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on lipotoxicity and β-cell regeneration data

claim: The high-dose dimerizer treatment resulted in >85% ablation of β-cell mass in P-AdnTg/+ mice at week 2.
source: As in the P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice, the high-dose dimerizer treatment resulted in >85% ablation of β-cell mass in P-AdnTg/+ mice at week 2 (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: In contrast to the prolonged β-cell loss in the P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice from week 5 to week 10, the P-AdnTg/+ β-cell area showed a significant recovery in β-cell mass during this period.
source: In contrast to the prolonged β-cell loss in the P-Adn+/+ and P-Adn−/− mice from week 5 to week 10 (Figure 1A), the P-AdnTg/+ β-cell area showed a significant recovery in β-cell mass during this period.
evidence: Supported by β-cell mass quantitation data

claim: The transgenic mice restored their islet mass to 29% of the WT controls that did not suffer β-cell ablation.
source: The transgenic mice restored their islet mass to 29% of the WT controls that did not suffer β-cell ablation (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The recovery of β-cell mass in P-AdnTg/+ mice was preceded by improvements in both the systemic lipid metabolism and the local islet lipotoxicity.
source: Importantly, the recovery of β-cell mass in P-AdnTg/+ mice was preceded by improvements in both the systemic lipid metabolism (Figure 5B–D) and the local islet lipotoxicity (Figure 6), potentially supporting a causal relationship of adiponectin-mediated lipid improvements leading to islet mass recovery.
evidence: Supported by temporal relationship between lipid improvements and β-cell mass recovery

claim: With the partially restored β-cell mass, P-AdnTg/+ mice significantly down-regulated their fasting blood glucose level to 199 ± 21 mg/dl.
source: With the partially restored β-cell mass, P-AdnTg/+ mice significantly down-regulated their fasting blood glucose level to 199 ± 21 mg/dl (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The restoration to euglycemia was observed in both female and aged male P-AdnTg/+ mice, supporting a sex- and age-independent effect of adiponectin in β-cell regeneration.
source: The restoration to euglycemia was observed in both female (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) and aged male P-AdnTg/+ mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B), supporting a sex- and age-independent effect of adiponectin in β-cell regeneration.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and 2B

claim: The P-AdnTg/+ mice displayed significant improvements in glucose tolerance.
source: We further examined the adiponectin-driven improvements in glucose metabolism and β-cell function in the P-AdnTg/+ mice. The mice displayed significant improvements in glucose tolerance (Figure 7C), fasting insulin, and in vivo GSIS (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7C

claim: The P-AdnTg/+ mice displayed significant improvements in fasting insulin and in vivo GSIS.
source: We further examined the adiponectin-driven improvements in glucose metabolism and β-cell function in the P-AdnTg/+ mice. The mice displayed significant improvements in glucose tolerance (Figure 7C), fasting insulin, and in vivo GSIS (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 3

claim: The P-AdnTg/+ islets showed an ∼fivefold increase in insulin secretion under both basal conditions and upon exposure to elevated glucose levels.
source: The P-AdnTg/+ islets showed an ∼fivefold increase in insulin secretion under both basal conditions and upon exposure to elevated glucose levels (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by in vitro GSIS data shown in Figure 7E

claim: The improvement in insulin secretion could be attributed to increases in both overall islet insulin content (1.7-fold) and exocytic activity (2.2-fold).
source: This improvement could be attributed to increases in both overall islet insulin content (1.7-fold, Figure 7—figure supplement 4B) and exocytic activity (2.2-fold, Figure 7—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4B and 4C

claim: Five weeks post ablation, P-AdnTg/+ mice showed higher ratios of Ki-67-positive cells in insulin-positive cells than seen in the islets of P-Adn+/+ or WT mice.
source: Five weeks post ablation, P-AdnTg/+ mice showed higher ratios of Ki-67-positive (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 5A) and BrdU-positive (Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 5B) cells in insulin-positive cells than seen in the islets of P-Adn+/+ or WT mice.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 5A

claim: Five weeks post ablation, P-AdnTg/+ mice showed higher ratios of BrdU-positive cells in insulin-positive cells than seen in the islets of P-Adn+/+ or WT mice.
source: Five weeks post ablation, P-AdnTg/+ mice showed higher ratios of Ki-67-positive (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 5A) and BrdU-positive (Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 5B) cells in insulin-positive cells than seen in the islets of P-Adn+/+ or WT mice.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 5B

claim: The potent adiponectin-driven improvements in systemic lipid metabolism and amelioration of local lipotoxicity may be an important facilitative component towards β-cell proliferation and may contribute to the eventual recovery of islet mass.
source: The potent adiponectin-driven improvements in systemic lipid metabolism and amelioration of local lipotoxicity may be an important facilitative component towards β-cell proliferation and may contribute to the eventual recovery of islet mass.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the lipid metabolism, lipotoxicity, and β-cell proliferation data

claim: When insulin levels decrease by >90% after intensive β-cell loss, adiponectin ensures the minimal homeostasis for lipid metabolism.
source: In this study, we uncover for the first time a pathological condition under which adiponectin is indispensable for survival. When insulin levels decrease by >90% after intensive β-cell loss, adiponectin ensures the minimal homeostasis for lipid metabolism.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing essential role of adiponectin under insulinopenic conditions

claim: Adiponectin mediates lipid uptake specifically in subcutaneous WAT, but not in epididymal WAT.
source: Consistent with insulin action promoting lipid storage in adipose tissue, adiponectin exerts a similar effect on lipid uptake, but does so by distinct mechanisms. First, adiponectin mediates lipid uptake specifically in subcutaneous WAT, but not in epididymal WAT.
evidence: Supported by tissue-specific lipid uptake data

claim: Hepatic VLDL secretion and fatty acid metabolism are unchanged in adiponectin null mice under insulinopenic conditions.
source: Hepatic VLDL secretion and fatty acid metabolism are unchanged.
evidence: Supported by tyloxapol injection data and liver gene expression data

claim: Adiponectin regulates neither lipoprotein lipase activity under insulinopenic conditions nor the intracellular translocation of fatty acids.
source: Second, adiponectin regulates neither lipoprotein lipase activity under insulinopenic conditions nor the intracellular translocation of fatty acids.
evidence: Supported by lipoprotein lipase activity assay and fatty acid transporter expression data

claim: Caveolin-1 is reduced in adiponectin null mice, thereby reducing endocytosis of lipids.
source: Rather, caveolin-1 is reduced, thereby reducing endocytosis of lipids.
evidence: Supported by caveolin-1 immunofluorescence and electron microscopy data

claim: Adiponectin knockout mice with insulin deficiency recapitulate the lipodystrophic phenotypes reported in caveolin-1 null mice, including impaired triglyceride clearance, hyper-triglyceridemia, adipocyte hypotrophy, without a change in lipoprotein lipase activity.
source: This is in agreement with our previous reports on caveolin-1 knockout mice, which show significantly lower body weight and fat mass than wild-type controls under both regular chow and high-fat diet regimen (Razani et al., 2002; Wernstedt Asterholm et al., 2012). Moreover, our adiponectin knockout mice with insulin deficiency recapitulate the lipodystrophic phenotypes reported in caveolin-1 null mice, including impaired triglyceride clearance, hyper-triglyceridemia, adipocyte hypotrophy, without a change in lipoprotein lipase activity (Razani et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by comparison with published data on caveolin-1 null mice and citations to Razani et al., 2002; Wernstedt Asterholm et al., 2012

claim: Adiponectin potentiates insulin signaling and the suppression on lipolysis mediated by the trace levels of insulin present.
source: Third, adiponectin potentiates insulin signaling and the suppression on lipolysis mediated by the trace levels of insulin present.
evidence: Supported by insulin signaling and lipolysis suppression data

claim: In cases where both insulin and adiponectin are depleted, fat mass becomes critically low, accompanied by exceedingly high triglycerides and ketone bodies in circulation, resulting in major mortality.
source: In cases where both insulin and adiponectin are depleted, fat mass becomes critically low, accompanied by exceedingly high triglycerides and ketone bodies in circulation, resulting in major mortality.
evidence: Supported by survival, fat mass, triglyceride, and ketone body data

claim: Massive pancreatic β-cell failure leads to hypoinsulinemia and dyslipidemia.
source: Our findings also underscore adiponectin as a messenger for the crosstalk between adipose tissue and pancreatic β-cells, especially under insulinopenic conditions. Massive pancreatic β-cell failure leads to hypoinsulinemia and dyslipidemia (Dunn, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dunn, 1992

claim: The ensuing aggravated lipotoxicity further impairs β-cell function and survival.
source: The ensuing aggravated lipotoxicity further impairs β-cell function and survival (Lupi et al., 2002; Kusminski et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lupi et al., 2002; Kusminski et al., 2009

claim: Adiponectin can disrupt the vicious cycle of β-cell failure at multiple levels and, in so doing, promote potent regenerative effects on functional β-cell mass.
source: Our findings demonstrate that adiponectin can disrupt this vicious cycle at multiple levels and, in so doing, promote potent regenerative effects on functional β-cell mass.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing adiponectin's effects on lipid metabolism and β-cell regeneration

claim: Adiponectin improves lipid storage in adipose tissue and improves systemic lipid metabolism.
source: Adiponectin improves lipid storage in adipose tissue and improves systemic lipid metabolism.
evidence: Supported by lipid uptake and systemic lipid metabolism data

claim: The general improvements in dyslipidemia may contribute, at least in part, to the reduction of β-cell lipotoxicity in the adiponectin overexpressing mouse, as reflected by ceramide measurements.
source: These general improvements in dyslipidemia may contribute, at least in part, to the reduction of β-cell lipotoxicity in the adiponectin overexpressing mouse, as reflected by ceramide measurements.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on lipid metabolism and ceramide data

claim: Overexpression of adiponectin is sufficient to regenerate β-cells and regain glycemic control.
source: Overexpression of adiponectin is sufficient to regenerate β-cells and regain glycemic control.
evidence: Supported by β-cell mass recovery and glucose control data in adiponectin transgenic mice

claim: The major impediments for effective β-cell regeneration may not only relate to the inherently low proliferation rate of β-cells, but also due to the systemic highly lipotoxic environment due to severe hyperlipidemia, both in type 1 diabetes as well as late stage type 2 diabetes.
source: The major impediments for effective β-cell regeneration may not only relate to the inherently low proliferation rate of β-cells, but also due to the systemic highly lipotoxic environment due to severe hyperlipidemia, both in type 1 diabetes as well as late stage type 2 diabetes.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings and established knowledge about β-cell regeneration

claim: In vitro experiments have provided strong evidence that lipotoxicity can impair β-cell function and survival.
source: In vitro experiments have provided strong evidence that lipotoxicity can impair β-cell function and survival (Maedler et al., 2001; Rakatzi et al., 2004; Hoppa et al., 2009; Holland et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maedler et al., 2001; Rakatzi et al., 2004; Hoppa et al., 2009; Holland et al., 2011

claim: Pancreatic islets transplanted into the hepatic portal area were destroyed by the local hyperlipidemic environment in rats.
source: Unger and colleagues demonstrated in rats that pancreatic islets transplanted into the hepatic portal area were destroyed by the local hyperlipidemic environment (Lee et al., 2007) and islets from Zucker diabetic fatty (ZDF) rats are subject to lipotoxic destruction via ceramide (Shimabukuro et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2007 and Shimabukuro et al., 1998

claim: Wild-type islets develop ceramide-induced impairments in islet function under hyperlipidemic/hyperglycemic conditions.
source: Poitout and colleagues have established that wild-type islets similarly develop ceramide-induced impairments in islet function under hyperlipidemic/hyperglycemic conditions (Kelpe et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelpe et al., 2003

claim: The prolonged β-cell loss in adiponectin wild-type and adiponectin null mice is unlikely due to prolonged exposure to dimerizer, which has a half-life in mice of ∼5 hr.
source: In the PANIC-ATTAC model, the prolonged β-cell loss in adiponectin wild-type and adiponectin null mice is unlikely due to prolonged exposure to dimerizer, which has a half-life in mice of ∼5 hr.
evidence: Inferred from the dimerizer half-life and the timing of β-cell loss

claim: The prolonged β-cell loss is the result of glucotoxicity, lipotoxicity, oxidative stress, and/or ER stress.
source: Rather, this is the result of glucotoxicity, lipotoxicity, oxidative stress, and/or ER stress.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental conditions and established knowledge about β-cell stress

claim: No differences in oxidative stress and ER stress markers were detected between adiponectin wild-type and transgenic adiponectin overexpressing mice in the PANIC-ATTAC islets.
source: In the PANIC-ATTAC islets, we did not detect any differences in oxidative stress and ER stress markers between adiponectin wild-type and transgenic adiponectin overexpressing mice (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (not shown)

claim: Differences at the level of lipotoxic intermediates were seen in the islet ceramide assays that revealed a reduction of lipotoxic ceramides as well as their precursors and derivatives.
source: However, we did see differences at the level of lipotoxic intermediates as judged by the results from the islet ceramide assays that revealed a reduction of lipotoxic ceramides as well as their precursors and derivatives.
evidence: Supported by sphingolipid mass spectrometry data

claim: The improved microenvironment allows for increased recovery of islet mass.
source: Ultimately, this improved microenvironment allows for increased recovery of islet mass.
evidence: Inferred from the lipotoxicity reduction and β-cell mass recovery data
